narration: The Fishermen's Horse
This is Chaiti Ghoda Nacha. 10th century to present.
on_screen: Title card: Chaiti Ghoda Nacha · India · 10th century to present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance is rooted in the Kaibarta Gita, a 15th-century text by Achutananda Das which traces the worship of Goddess Baseli to the 10th century.
Mythologically, it commemorates a horse gifted by Lord Rama to the Keot fishermen.
In the 20th century, it served as a covert tool for freedom fighters to organize against British rule.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance is performed during the Baseli Puja, spanning from Chaitra Purnima to Baisakha Purnima.
It is a ritual of the fisherman community to honor their patron goddess and celebrate their mythological lineage.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: A dancer enters the hollow bamboo frame of the dummy horse, which is suspended by straps over the shoulders.
The movement mimics the gait of a horse, coordinated with the Rauta and Rautani who sing and dance alongside.
The performance involves rhythmic footwork synchronized with the dhola drum and mahuri melodies.
Watch for Ghoda Nacha.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The primary instruments are the dhola (a traditional drum) and the mahuri (a double-reed wind instrument).
The music consists of folk songs performed by the Rauta and Rautani, often involving call-and-response or narrative storytelling.
Listen for the Dhola, Mahuri.
The sound is characterized by the high-pitched, piercing melody of the mahuri wind instrument over the deep, resonant rhythmic patterns of the dhola drum, accompanied by vocal storytelling.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The central prop is a bamboo horse frame dyed with red clay and fitted with a wooden head.
Dancers wear traditional Odia folk attire; the Rautani wears female clothing and ornaments.
The setting is typically an open village square or temple courtyard during the months of March to May.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Utsav Charan Das of Choudwar is the most prominent figure, awarded the Padma Shri in 2020 for sixty years of dedication to the dance and its use in social awareness campaigns.
While primarily associated with the Keot fishermen of coastal Odisha, specific accounts mention the Kujanga area as a site where the dance was historically used for political mobilization.
The dance belongs to the Shakta tradition of Hinduism, specifically the worship of Baseli, and is passed down through the Keot (Kaibarta) aboriginal fisherman tribes.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Chaiti Ghoda Nacha is sibling of Poikaal Kuthirai Aattam: Another Indian dummy horse dance tradition from Tamil Nadu.
Chaiti Ghoda Nacha is sibling of Kachhi Ghodi: A similar dummy horse folk dance from Rajasthan.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: The horse frame is a ritual object worshipped for eight days before dancing begins; the wooden head is considered a sacred relic and is stored in a temple between seasons.

scenes.title: Until next time
narration: Witness the transformation of bamboo and clay into a sacred stallion as Odisha's fishermen dance to honor a goddess and a legendary gift from a king.
